library(jsonlite)

read_json5_clean <- function (arg0_path) {
  txt <- readLines(arg0_path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  clean_txt <- gsub("//.*$", "", txt, perl = TRUE)
  fromJSON(paste(clean_txt, collapse = "\n"), simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

mod_data <- read_json5_clean("yayoi_and_kofun_japan.json5")
sett_data <- read_json5_clean("yayoi_and_kofun_japan_settlements.json")
ledger_data <- read_json5_clean("yayoi_and_kofun_japan_source_ledger.json5")

reg_names <- c(

# Abstract

This gazetteer catalogues 714 nucleated settlements, moated enclosures, regional chieftain centres and early imperial palace complexes active across the Japanese archipelago between 250BC and 650AD (covering 390.852 km² across thirteen historical territories). Synthesising national archaeological registries, the Rekihaku radiocarbon database, excavation monographs and historical demographic analyses [@Imamura1996Prehistoric; @Kito2000Jinko; @Farris2009DailyLife; @Kudo2023JapanC14], the register encompasses every primary central place of the protohistoric era: the twin seventh-century Asuka-Naniwa administrative capitals of Asuka (42k) and Naniwa (35k), the fifth-century Kawachi monumental centre at Mozu-Furuichi (22k), the third-century Early Kofun royal complex at Makimuku (15k), regional chieftain hubs at Kibi-Tsukuriyama (14k), Dazaifu (14k), Naka-Hie (10k), Izumo (9,5k), Sakitama (8,5k) and Mitsudera (7,5k), alongside major Yayoi moated centres including Yoshinogari (5,4k), Karako-Kagi (5,0k), Asahi (4,5k), Mikumo-Minamishoji (4,2k) and Ikegami-Sone (3,5k). Across the 714 catalogued centres, the gazetteer records 1.943 settlement-year population observations spanning 250BC to 650AD (averaging 2,72 observations per centre). Alongside the 714 catalogued settlements, the regional source ledger records 4.002 excluded duplicate entries, isolated artefact findspots and close-pair mortuary features out of 4.716 total evaluated candidates.

# Background

Settlement morphology in protohistoric Japan reflected the evolution of agricultural technology, demographic pressure and political centralisation [@Imamura1996Prehistoric; @Hudson1992Rice; @Farris2009DailyLife]. In the Early Yayoi period, communities inhabited unfortified hamlets positioned directly adjacent to irrigable back-swamp paddies, as seen at Itazuke in Fukuoka and Nabata in Saga [@Imamura1996Prehistoric].

By the Middle Yayoi period, rising population density and competition over alluvial land and imported bronze regalia prompted the construction of defensive moated settlements (*kan'go shuraku*) [@Imamura1996Prehistoric; @West2024Agentbased]. These settlements featured deep V-shaped ditches, timber palisades, elevated watchtowers and zoned precincts separating residential pit-dwellings, raised-floor granaries and jar-burial cemeteries, exemplified by Yoshinogari on the Saga Plain and Karako-Kagi in the Nara Basin [@Imamura1996Prehistoric; @West2024Agentbased]. Concurrently, communities established fortified hilltop redoubts (*koshin shuraku*) overlooking maritime coastal corridors [@Imamura1996Prehistoric].

The transition to the Kofun period witnessed the decline of moated villages and the rise of sprawling agrarian lowlands commanded by monumental burial tumuli and elite residential compounds (*gokan*) surrounded by stone-faced ditches, as excavated at Mitsudera in Gunma [@Imamura1996Prehistoric]. In the seventh century, the consolidation of the imperial Yamato state culminated in the construction of permanent capital cities featuring palace enclosures, aristocratic mansions, Buddhist temples and grid-aligned markets in the Asuka Valley and at the port of Naniwa on Osaka Bay [@Farris2009DailyLife; @Kito2000Jinko].

# Methodology

Settlement records were constructed by cross-referencing the national site compendia of the Japanese Archaeological Association, the Agency for Cultural Affairs, municipal excavation reports and historical demographic syntheses [@Kudo2023JapanC14; @Imamura1996Prehistoric; @Farris2009DailyLife]. All 714 catalogued settlements carry geographical coordinates and assign to one of the thirteen historical territorial masks.

In the regional source ledger, 4.002 candidate entries were excluded as duplicate historical aliases, isolated ceramic and lithic findspots lacking structural residential evidence, or close-pair satellite mounds situated within 5 km of primary catalogued centres [@Imamura1996Prehistoric]. For example, satellite tumuli surrounding the Daisenryo and Konda-Gobyoyama mounds were consolidated into the Mozu-Furuichi Core complex, preserving canonical territorial entries with documented longitudinal spans.

# Testing and Validation

Ledger reconciliation confirms 714 included settlements and 4.002 excluded candidate entries (4.716 total evaluated entities, with zero unaccounted records). All 714 settlements possess geographic coordinates and non-zero population records across their active historical spans. Figure \ref{fig:sett-gazetteer} displays the rank-size distribution and the fifteen leading urban and proto-urban centres of the archipelago.

# Results

## Top 45 Settlements by Peak Population

Table \ref{tab:top45-japan} presents the top 45 settlements in the gazetteer ordered by peak documented population, illustrating the dominance of the Yamato imperial capitals, the Middle Kofun Kawachi complexes, and regional chieftain centres across Kibi, Northern Kyushu and Kanto.

```{r tab-top45, results='asis'}
fmt_coord <- function(x) gsub("[.]", ",", format(round(as.numeric(x), 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE))

get_pop_str <- function(e, y) {
  v <- e[["population"]][[y]]
  if (is.null(v)) return("-")
  viscount_fmt_pop(v)
}

peaks <- vapply(sett_data, function(e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))), numeric(1))
ord <- order(peaks, decreasing = TRUE)
top_n <- min(45L, length(ord))

rows <- lapply(sett_data[ord[seq_len(top_n)]], function(e) {
  yrs <- as.integer(names(e[["population"]]))
  pks <- as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))
  pk_y <- names(e[["population"]])[which.max(pks)]
  pk_v <- max(pks)
  pk_lbl <- ifelse(as.numeric(pk_y) < 0, paste0(abs(as.numeric(pk_y)), "BC"), paste0(pk_y, "AD"))
  min_lbl <- ifelse(min(yrs) < 0, paste0(abs(min(yrs)), "BC"), paste0(min(yrs), "AD"))
  max_lbl <- ifelse(max(yrs) < 0, paste0(abs(max(yrs)), "BC"), paste0(max(yrs), "AD"))
  reg_label <- if (e[["region_id"]] %in% names(reg_names)) reg_names[[e[["region_id"]]]] else e[["region_id"]]
  data.frame(
    Settlement = e[["name"]],
    Province = reg_label,
    Coords = paste0(fmt_coord(e[["coords"]][[1]]), ", ", fmt_coord(e[["coords"]][[2]])),
    Span = paste0(min_lbl, "-", max_lbl),
    P1AD = get_pop_str(e, "1"),
    P300AD = get_pop_str(e, "300"),
    P500AD = get_pop_str(e, "500"),
    P650AD = get_pop_str(e, "650"),
    Peak = paste0(viscount_fmt_pop(pk_v), " (", pk_lbl, ")"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
top_df <- do.call(rbind, rows)
rownames(top_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  top_df,
  "Top 45 settlements in Yayoi and Kofun Japan ordered by peak documented population (n=714 total sites).",
  c("Settlement", "Province", "Lat, Lon", "Span", "1AD", "300AD", "500AD", "650AD", "Peak (Year)"),
  list(label = "tab:top45-japan", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 26L)
)
```

## Sub-Regional Distribution and Ledger Exclusions

Table \ref{tab:regsum-japan} summarises the distribution of catalogued settlements across all thirteen historical territories alongside their leading centres. Tohoku leads all territories with 136 catalogued settlements, followed by Kanto (90), Kinai (82), Northern Kyushu (71), Hokuriku (56) and Tokai (50). Table \ref{tab:excluded-japan} details the leading 30 of 4.002 excluded candidate entries in the regional source ledger.

```{r tab-regsum, results='asis'}
reg_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)

sum_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function(rk) {
  sub_e <- Filter(function(e) identical(e[["region_id"]], rk), sett_data)
  max_nm <- "-"
  if (length(sub_e) > 0) {
    pks <- vapply(sub_e, function(e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))), numeric(1))
    idx_m <- which.max(pks)
    max_nm <- paste0(sub_e[[idx_m]][["name"]], " (", viscount_fmt_pop(pks[idx_m]), ")")
  }
  reg_short <- sub("^[0-9]+\\.\\s*", "", mod_data$regions[[rk]]$name)
  data.frame(
    Territory = gsub("&", "and", reg_short, fixed = TRUE),
    Sites = as.character(length(sub_e)),
    Lead = max_nm,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
sum_df <- do.call(rbind, sum_rows)
rownames(sum_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  sum_df,
  "Settlement counts and leading archaeological centres across the thirteen Japanese territories (714 total sites).",
  c("Territory", "Catalogued Sites", "Leading Centre (Peak)"),
  list(label = "tab:regsum-japan", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 20L)
)
```

```{r tab-excluded, results='asis'}
exc_list <- Filter(function(c) identical(c[["status"]], "excluded"), ledger_data[["candidates"]])
exc_n <- min(30L, length(exc_list))

exc_rows <- lapply(exc_list[seq_len(exc_n)], function(c) {
  just <- as.character(c[["justification"]])
  just <- gsub("([0-9]+)\\.([0-9]+)\\s*km", "\\1,\\2 km", just, perl = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    Candidate = c[["name"]],
    Territory = c[["country"]],
    Category = "Duplicate or satellite feature",
    Justification = just,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
exc_df <- do.call(rbind, exc_rows)
rownames(exc_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  exc_df,
  "Leading 30 of 4.002 excluded candidate entries in the Yayoi and Kofun source ledger, consolidated into canonical settlements.",
  c("Candidate", "Territory", "Classification", "Consolidation Justification"),
  list(label = "tab:excluded-japan", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Limitations

Two spatial factors affect protohistoric settlement analysis in this gazetteer. First, major political capitals such as the Asuka complex and Naniwa encompassed multiple palace iterations, aristocratic residences and Buddhist temples dispersed across several square kilometres rather than enclosed within a single continuous stone circuit. These dispersed royal compounds are aggregated into unified metropolitan entities to avoid artificial fragmentation of contiguous court populations [@Farris2009DailyLife; @Kito2000Jinko]. Second, while nucleated agricultural villages and moated enclosures are recorded in detail, temporary hunting lodges, seasonal fishing encampments and shifting dry-field swidden plots are represented through rural territorial totals rather than discrete urban points [@Imamura1996Prehistoric; @Koyama1978Jomon].
